summary:
Jamaica's Offences Against the Person Act punishes buggery by up to 10 years' hard labour, and the US State Department's 2023 human rights report confirms that the provision criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. The same report states that no statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and that individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender. A trans visitor therefore arrives with no legal gender recognition, no statutory protection against discrimination, and no carve-out from the sexual-offences regime.

State protection is documented as absent. The US Department of Justice country packet (2013) records that LGBT victims are reluctant to report crimes because police leak incident details, fail to investigate LGBT violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights' report of 10 August 2012 on the situation of human rights in Jamaica finds the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject to be deplorable. Human Rights Watch, in a letter of 30 November 2004 accompanying its report Hated to Death, documented police harassment of gay men and HIV/AIDS outreach workers, community and family violence carried out with impunity, and official indifference. An Amnesty International urgent appeal of 4 June 2006 reported vigilante violence together with police ill-treatment or torture of LGBT people. In September 2019 police stated they could not provide protection to LGBT Jamaicans after Montego Bay's mayor and a councilor blocked the local cultural centre's use by the local LGBT group and other venues cancelled reservations, forcing the October 2019 Pride events to be cancelled.

Custody carries documented identity-targeted violence. The 2023 State Department report records that prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived LGBTQI identity, in significantly overcrowded facilities where Tower Street maximum-security cells held three times their capacity under harsh, life-threatening conditions; a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. A 2018 study by University of the West Indies lecturer Carla Moore, reported on 5 February 2019, found that prisoners perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender are isolated in Jamaica's penal institutions, that rehabilitation opportunities for them are basically non-existent, that other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners, and that no specialised housing policy is documented; it estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities and reported prevalent corrective rape of lesbians. J-FLAG reported in 2012 harassment of gay and lesbian patients by hospital and prison staff and numerous reports of violence against gay inmates by wardens and other inmates, with few seeking recourse through the prison system.

Jamaica recognises no marriage or partnership between women. The Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (Constitutional Amendment) Act 2011 explicitly bars recognition of same-sex marriage and any other kind of union. In July 2019 Maurice Tomlinson petitioned the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights to rule that Section 18(2) of the Constitution contravenes the American Convention on Human Rights and to order repeal and recognition of his Canadian marriage, and a separate July 2019 petition asks that Jamaica allow naturalisation of same-sex spouses of Jamaican citizens on the same terms as heterosexual spouses. In 2019 both Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Peter Phillips announced opposition to legalising same-sex marriage. Lesbian civil ceremonies have taken place, including the 2012 celebration in Jamaica of Jamaican-born Nicole Y. Dennis-Benn and Emma Benn, legally married in New York, but Jamaica recognises no legal basis for partnerships between women.

Documented lethal violence against gender-nonconforming people is dated. In July 2013 a mob in St. James stabbed to death Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old, and the case remained unsolved with no arrests as of 2022; the most recent documented killing of a gender-nonconforming person in these sources is from July 2013, and no later instance is documented. J-FLAG data recorded 68 reports of sexually motivated harassment or abuse in 2012, 53 assault cases and at least two killings, borne most heavily by people aged 18 to 29; these are raw counts with no population denominator and do not measure per-capita risk. J-FLAG co-founder Brian Williamson was stabbed to death in June 2004, with a crowd outside his home celebrating and chanting slurs.

An amicus brief filed in February 2024 in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights argues that continued criminalisation and systemic discrimination leave transgender Jamaicans exposed to housing insecurity and to educational and employment insecurity. The UNDP national survey Being LGBT in Jamaica (March 2023), a survey of LGBT Jamaicans rather than transgender people alone, carries dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care, quantifying lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop. In January 2019 the Director of Tourism, Donovan White, said gay tourists are welcome and that Jamaicans harboured no open hostility toward gay visitors.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion data is consistently hostile and is dated in each instance: 96 per cent opposed legalising homosexual relations in 2001; 70 per cent said in 2008 that homosexuals are not entitled to the same basic rights; 85.2 per cent opposed legalising homosexuality among consenting adults in a 2010 survey; 88 per cent disapproved of homosexuality in a 2016 J-FLAG poll; and 2023 polling indicates at least 60 per cent oppose acceptance of homosexuality. In 2013 the majority of LGBTQ people in the country said they faced homophobic violence in public. In 2012 about a third of the population, over 900,000 Jamaicans, believed the government was not doing enough to protect LGBT people from violence and discrimination.

The UN Human Rights Committee's 2011 review regretted virulent lyrics by musicians and entertainers that incite violence against homosexuals and urged Jamaica to investigate and sanction those responsible. Dancehall artists including Buju Banton, Beenie Man, Bounty Killer, Elephant Man, Sizzla and Shabba Ranks have written or performed songs advocating attacks on gay and lesbian people, and a 2005 agreement between dancehall labels and groups such as OutRage! and the Stop Murder Music Coalition sought to end anti-gay lyrics in live performance.

Maurice Tomlinson sued Jamaican TV stations TVJ, PBCJ and CVM in 2012 for refusing to air a 30-second advertisement, Love and Respect, promoting recognition of LGBT people's humanity; the Constitutional Court ruled against him in November 2013, and the Court of Appeal heard the appeal in February 2016 with judgment reserved.

LGBT Jamaicans have fled abroad for safety: Maurice Tomlinson moved to Toronto in 2011 after death threats, Gareth Henry sought asylum in Canada in 2008, and Simone Edwards was granted asylum in the Netherlands in 2008.

University campuses have been sites of anti-LGBT violence. Students at UWI's Mona campus rioted in April 2006 while police protected a man chased across campus, and in November 2012 two campus security guards beat a reportedly gay student seeking refuge from a mob, after which the University of Technology established a working group on intolerance and bullying.

In January 2018 Jamaica barred entry to Steven Anderson, a Holocaust-denying anti-gay pastor from Arizona, after an outcry from activists; he said he was told at the airport he would not be allowed into the country.

The Inter-American Commission's 2012 report also covers citizen security, police killings including the May 2010 operation, and the administration of justice, with civil-society input from Jamaicans for Justice and J-FLAG.
localsOnly:
The amicus brief of February 2024 documents that transgender Jamaicans face housing insecurity and educational and employment insecurity under the discrimination regime, conditions that fall on residents rather than visitors.

The UNDP survey Being LGBT in Jamaica (March 2023) includes a dedicated chapter on transgender access to health care, quantifying service exclusion for residents under the criminalisation backdrop.

For residents in custody, the 2018 University of the West Indies study found isolation inside penal institutions, essentially non-existent rehabilitation opportunities, severely curtailed movement and limited access to resources because of entrenched homophobia and transphobia, and prevalent corrective rape of lesbians; no specialised housing policy is documented. J-FLAG's 2012 reporting records harassment of patients by hospital staff and violence against inmates by wardens, with few residents seeking recourse through the prison system.

J-FLAG, founded in December 1998, operates underground and anonymously as Jamaica's first LGBT human rights organisation. Quality of Citizenship Jamaica, founded in 2013, worked to create safe spaces for LGBT women, youth and transgender people before ending operations in 2018.

Dr. J. Carolyn Gomes resigned as head of Jamaicans for Justice in 2013 after nationwide pushback on sexual-education leaflets for adolescents that mentioned anal sex.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific violence rate with a denominator appears in these sources. The J-FLAG figures for 2012 are raw counts of reports, assaults and killings without a population base, so they cannot be read as a per-capita risk measure, and no source compares a transgender-specific rate against Jamaica's general homicide rate.

Whether the buggery provision has been used in prosecution, and with what sentences, is not sourced. The penalty of up to 10 years' hard labour is stated in a 2013 country packet and again in the 2023 human rights report, but no case-level enforcement data is available here.

The status of the Dwayne Jones case is unresolved after 2022: the sources record no arrests as of that year and no later documentation of the investigation.

The sources date from 2004 to February 2024, and nothing later is available. Several findings, including the Human Rights Watch letter of 2004, the Amnesty International appeal of 2006 and the Inter-American Commission report of 2012, describe conditions at those dates rather than the present.

The survey evidence is LGBT-wide rather than transgender-specific: the UNDP national survey of March 2023 covers LGBT Jamaicans, and the polling series measures attitudes to homosexuality generally. No current survey of transgender people alone is sourced.

Whether any reform of legal gender recognition or anti-discrimination legislation is pending is not sourced. Airport screening, document-marker and border-inspection treatment of transgender travellers is not addressed by any source here.
